facts.text: Star-writer-director Richard Gabai says he wrote this on a typewriter over a weekend, then raised $40,000 from ten investors at $4,000 each.
Richard Gabai was inspired by acting in David DeCoteau's Nightmare Sisters, where he was told the budget was $40,000. DeCoteau later admitted it cost only $8,000.
Troy Donahue, the 1950s teen idol playing Sid Witherspoon, shot all of his scenes for this movie in a single day.
Troy Donahue and Doug McClure were the inspiration for Troy McClure, the washed-up actor on The Simpsons, which premiered the same year as this film.
Nightmare Sisters (1988), where Richard Gabai played Kevin, was shot in four days for about $40,000 and starred Linnea Quigley, Brinke Stevens and Michelle Bauer: the same scream queens as here.
The whole movie was shot in just five days. It was written and filmed under the title The Last Party.
Michelle Bauer, who plays Muffin, was pregnant during filming. IMDb says three months; another review site says six.
The film became a late-night staple on USA Network's USA Up All Night, airing from July 1990 and many times through 1997.
B&S About Movies notes that Michelle Bauer and Linnea Quigley play college students here even though they were thirtysomething scream queens when this was shot.
Both fraternity houses are the same house: the front yard played the Zeta house, the backyard the Lambda house. Richard Gabai lived there in college.
Troy Donahue, who plays Sid Witherspoon, was once a Warner Bros. star: A Summer Place (1959) won him a Golden Globe, and TV's Surfside 6 gave him 71 episodes as Sandy Winfield II.
Richard Gabai also wrote the film's songs and performed them with his power-pop band The Checks. Brian Orndorf says the montages double as promotion for the band.
Prism Entertainment released it in summer 1989, and it did good business on VHS. That success landed Richard Gabai an agent.
Reviewing the 2025 Blu-ray, critic Brian Orndorf called it "completely laugh-free and painfully low-budget," and said it is "more Ed Wood" than Revenge of the Nerds.
This was Richard Gabai's filmmaking debut. Brian Orndorf writes that its small following grew out of early-morning basic-cable airings in the 1990s.
Richard Gabai hid a private joke: the expiration date on the fire extinguisher prop is his own birthday, February 14, 1964.
After seeing ten minutes of this film, producer Menahem Golan financed Richard Gabai's next movie, Virgin High, for $150,000, then sold it to Columbia for $750,000.
A gay men's magazine prop had a nude spread of actor Kevin M. Glover (Cliff). Richard Gabai spotted it, pulled the pages and quietly told him; Glover didn't seem to care.
Kevin M. Glover (Cliff) and Tantala Ray (Vanna) both also appeared in adult films.
Robert Dorfmann, who plays Chip, is credited here as Robert Mann. In the sequel he used his real name.
Reviewer Brian Orndorf says the 1995 sequel had a noticeably bigger budget and more shooting days than this five-day original, yet "the helmer's sense of humor doesn't receive an upgrade."
A sequel, Assault of the Party Nerds 2: The Heavy Petting Detective, followed in 1995, with Burt Ward and Linnea Quigley among the cast.
The sequel's cast includes Laugh-In veteran Arte Johnson and Tane McClure, who later played Elle's mom in Legally Blonde.
The film is referenced in the 2015 movie Dinosaur Island and in the 2003 documentary Sex at 24 Frames Per Second.
